artifacts.summary: Full implementation summary for the deploy-engine consolidation: one manifest-driven engine, idempotent load/resync/wipe, full-category content-hash verification, and the prose sweep correcting every stale reference to the retired engine.

completion_data.completion_summary: Retired the glob+allow-list load_all_globally deploy engine in favor of the single manifest-driven extension loader, reachable via the picker's [Reload All]/[Regenerate] entries and deploy-headless.sh's resync/--wipe modes. Extended post-load verification (verify.lua + verify-deploy.sh's new gate5) to declared-vs-deployed parity plus content-hash equality across all 11 provides.* categories. Corrected every stale prose reference to the retired engine and its Phase-2-retired per-category copier functions across 17 documentation/script files. Fixed a genuine regression found during the final verification-bar execution: a brand-new consuming repo's .syncprotect auto-seed step, present in the retired engine but missing from the new one, is now restored. This repository's own live .claude/ deploy passes verify-deploy.sh cleanly at 16/16 checks, 0 failures.

memory_candidates.content: In this repo's deploy-engine (lua/neotex/plugins/ai/shared/extensions/), manager.resync_all only resyncs extensions already marked 'active' in a target repo's project-root .claude-extensions.json state file. The historical glob-based load_all_globally engine (retired) was stateless and never wrote that file, so any target repo only ever deployed via the old engine has NO active-extension entries. A bulk-resync entry point (e.g. deploy-headless.sh's default invocation) must therefore force-load the baseline extension (e.g. 'core') first via manager.load(name, {force=true}) before calling resync_all, or it silently deploys zero files on first use against such a repo. Verified empirically: a bare resync_all against a from-scratch scratch git repo deployed 0 files; force-load-core-then-resync_all deployed 339.

When a Lua copy engine reads/writes files via vim.fn.readfile/writefile (line-array semantics, not raw byte streams), writefile() unconditionally appends a trailing newline after the last line unless called with the 'b' binary flag. A source file lacking a final trailing newline will therefore always gain one when copied through such an engine -- this is faithful copying BY THAT ENGINE'S OWN DEFINITION, not corruption. Any downstream content-hash/diff verifier built against the same copy engine must hash/compare the same line-joined representation (e.g. table.concat(vim.fn.readfile(path), '\n')) rather than raw file bytes, or it will report a false-positive 'content differs from source' finding on every such file, even on a completely clean deploy.

nvim --headless invocations in this environment can prepend a terminal OSC7 cwd-reporting escape sequence to the very first line of stdout, with no newline separator before the actual program output. A start-of-line-anchored grep pattern (e.g. grep -c '^TOKEN ') against captured $(nvim --headless ... 2>&1) output can silently match zero lines even when the token is genuinely present, because the escape sequence occupies column 1. Use unanchored grep (grep -c 'TOKEN ', grep -o 'TOKEN .*') when parsing headless-nvim stdout captured this way, and strip-to-first-match (bash's ${var#*TOKEN } not ${var#TOKEN }) when extracting the payload.

When retiring one of two independent bulk-sync/deploy mechanisms in favor of the other, check whether the retired one performed any first-run bootstrap side effect (e.g. auto-seeding a config file with a sane default) that the surviving mechanism never needed because the retired one always ran first historically. Retiring the mechanism that used to run first can silently drop that bootstrap step for any consumer that starts fresh with only the surviving mechanism, even though every already-established consumer (which already has the seeded artifact from a prior run) never notices the gap. Found via a from-scratch scratch-tree wipe+regenerate round-trip test specifically -- an already-deployed test repo would never have surfaced it.
